paragraphs: One ring per reactor thread, one reactor per core. Each reactor owns its ring, its SOREUSEPORT listener, its connections and its clients outright, so nothing is shared and nothing is locked - a request never leaves the core it arrived on, inbound and outbound alike. What makes that practical in .NET is that you do not give up the platform's async model to get it: handlers are ordinary async Task code, ring completions resume their continuations inline on the reactor thread, and a per-reactor SynchronizationContext catches everything that would otherwise escape - timers, HttpClient, Task.Run.…
ioxide hands you raw bytes and stays out of HTTP; when you want a framework on top, ioxide.Kestrel swaps the transport under an existing ASP.NET Core app with your endpoints unchanged.
